channel.title: Cadence Evidence — PT Research Signal
channel.description: Daily curated physical therapy & rehab research for clinicians. AI-scored signal from 56 sources.

item.title: Altered Cognitive Control and Cortical Oscillatory Dynamics in Athletes With ACL Reconstruction During Decision-Making Under Uncertainty.
item.description: In a controlled laboratory study of 90 open-skill athletes (45 non-ACLR, 45 ACLR), athletes with ACL reconstruction (ACLR) showed slower response times, lower accuracy (d = 0.75-1.09), and persistent alterations in cortical oscillatory mechanisms related to cognitive control, motor preparation, and attentional allocation during decision-making under uncertainty.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Diagnosis, Rehabilitation, and Return to Sport after Athletic Hamstring Injury: An ICCUS Society Consensus Statement.
item.description: An ICCUS Society consensus statement, derived from a modified Delphi process with 17 expert clinicians, achieved over 80% agreement on 54 statements across three domains for managing athletic hamstring injuries, emphasizing standardized terminology, individualized criterion-based rehabilitation, progressive tissue loading, and objective assessment for return-to-sport decisions.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Comparative study of therapeutic ultrasound and whole-body vibration as adjuncts to passive stretching on knee joint range of motion and functional ability in children with hemiplegic cerebral palsy: a randomized trial
item.description: A randomized trial with 60 children (4-6 years old) with hemiplegic cerebral palsy found that whole-body vibration (WBV) as an adjunct to passive stretching resulted in significantly greater improvements in active knee extension ROM (13.82% vs 7.05%) and Gross Motor Function Measure-88 scores (22.72% vs 11.32%) over 12 weeks compared to therapeutic ultrasound.
item.author: BMC Musculoskelet Disord

item.title: Effects of Exercise Type and Duration on Pain, Function, and Quality of Life in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review With Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis.
item.description: A Bayesian network meta-analysis of 35 trials (n=3808) found that short-term (≤12 weeks) combined aerobic and resistance exercise had the largest effects on pain (SMD = -0.937, low certainty), function (SMD = -0.590, low certainty), and quality of life (SMD = 0.663, low certainty) in patients with knee osteoarthritis.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Wearable-based digital metrics reveal dynamic dissociations between upper limb capacity and real-world use over the first six months after stroke
item.description: In 72 stroke patients over six months, wearable-based digital metrics revealed that upper limb activity capacity and real-world performance were correlated (Spearman's ρs = 0.45–0.78, p < 0.001) but their coupling weakened over time, with 52% of those improving on ARAT not improving their use ratio, indicating a dynamic dissociation.
item.author: J NeuroEng Rehabil

item.title: Exercise-based rehabilitation interventions for kinesiophobia after total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
item.description: Exercise-based rehabilitation significantly reduced kinesiophobia (SMD = -1.22, 95% CI [-1.72, -0.72]) and improved knee function (SMD = 1.19, 95% CI [0.67, 1.71]) in 1,096 patients after total knee arthroplasty, although certainty of evidence was low and heterogeneity was high.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Comparative Effects of Neurostimulation- and Technology-Augmented Robot-Assisted Training on Upper-Limb Motor Recovery After Stroke: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
item.description: A network meta-analysis of 103 trials (5,251 participants) found rTMS plus robot-assisted training (RAT) yielded the largest Fugl-Meyer Assessment for Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) estimate (MD 9.56, 95% CI 7.18-11.93 vs. usual care), followed by LFES plus RAT (MD 7.52), outperforming RAT alone (MD 3.83).
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Neurocognitive Factors in ACL Injury: The Missing Piece in Rehabilitation and Prevention? A Scoping Review.
item.description: A scoping review of 42 studies suggests that neurocognitive factors, including dual-task interference, visual attention, reaction time, and cognitive fatigue, are significant contributors to ACL injury and that integrating neurocognitive challenges into rehabilitation and RTS testing may help identify athletes at risk for secondary injury.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSpect): an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial
item.description: An international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomized controlled trial (PROSpect) found no evidence to support prone positioning or high-frequency oscillatory ventilation as first-line strategies to improve ventilator-free days in patients with early, moderate-to-severe pediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome.
item.author: The Lancet

item.title: Adding blood flow restriction to low-load resistance training for sarcopenia and cognitive function in oldest-old adults: an exploratory randomized controlled trial
item.description: An exploratory RCT (N=36) in oldest-old adults with sarcopenia and MCI found supervised low-load BFR-RT to be well-attended and safe, showing favorable changes in handgrip strength, 4-m walk time, verbal learning, and delayed recall compared to no exercise, but limited additional benefits over matched low-load RT.
item.author: BMC Geriatrics

item.title: Effects of chair-based exercise training on pulmonary function, exercise capacity, and quality of life in patients with acute exacerbation of COPD: A randomised controlled trial.
item.description: A randomized controlled trial of 30 AECOPD patients found chair-based exercise training significantly improved functional exercise capacity (6MWT distance: mean change 79.7m vs 28.8m, p=0.042), dyspnoea, and quality of life compared to breathing exercises alone.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Healthcare professionals' perceptions and experiences of promoting physical activity in persons with multiple sclerosis: a systematic review of qualitative evidence.
item.description: A systematic review of eight studies found that improving physical activity promotion in MS care requires MS-specific education and training for healthcare professionals, practical resources such as patient education materials and referral pathways, and stronger cross-sector coordination to sustain consistent practice.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Adherence System Usability Patient Experience and Psychosocial Impact in Robot Assisted Gait Neurorehabilitation A Cross Sectional Study.
item.description: A single-center observational study of 250 adults in robot-assisted gait neurorehabilitation found that greater attendance, usability, and rehabilitation experience were associated with a favorable psychosocial impact, with mean participation at 86.35% ± 8.38% and strong correlations (r s = 0.41 to 0.53) between adherence, system usability, rehabilitation experience, and psychosocial impact.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Gamified Versus Traditional Balance Training: Effects on Balance and Motivation in Collegiate Student-Athletes.
item.description: A quasi-experimental controlled trial of 30 collegiate athletes found that both gamified (Wii Fit) and traditional (wobble board) balance training significantly improved anterior reach and mSEBT composite scores compared to control (gamified: +21.6 ± 11.9 cm; traditional: +18.5 ± 14.6 cm; p < 0.01), with gamified training eliciting higher interest/enjoyment scores (5.0 ± 1.2 vs 3.2 ± 1.3; p < 0.01).
item.author: PubMed

item.title: What are the barriers and facilitators to engagement with physiotherapy among women experiencing adverse effects associated with menopause?
item.description: A qualitative study identified fatigue, cognitive issues, and low self-efficacy as barriers to physiotherapy engagement among 12 menopausal women with musculoskeletal pain in the UK. Facilitators included direct inquiry about menopause, feeling heard, individualized treatment, and education.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Investigating the Feasibility of Locomotor Training for Children Under 5 Years With Complex Neurodisabilties.
item.description: A 6-week locomotor training program, including partial body weight-supported treadmill training and overground walking in supported stepping devices, was found feasible and beneficial for 71 children (mean age 2.8 years) with neurodisabilities, showing improvements in Goal Attainment Scaling scores (12.8 to 56.2), Canadian Occupational Performance Measure, and mobility outcomes.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Treatment Planning in Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine: A Systematic Review.
item.description: A systematic review of 9 studies found that large language models (LLMs) showed promising capabilities in supporting rehabilitation treatment planning, with concordance up to 98.75% with expert opinion after review, and alignment with guidelines in musculoskeletal and cardiovascular rehabilitation. However, hallucinations were reported, underscoring the necessity of supervision.
item.author: PubMed

item.title: Effectiveness of Plyometric Exercises Versus Flatfoot Corrective Exercises on Balance and Foot Posture in Obese Children with a Flexible Flatfoot: A Comparative Study
item.description: A non-randomized comparative study (n=120) found that 8 weeks of plyometric training significantly improved balance (median path length: 30.39 cm vs. 37.45 cm, p<0.001) and foot posture (left foot, p=0.028) compared to flatfoot corrective exercises in obese children with flexible flatfoot.
item.author: medRxiv

item.title: A Retrospective Real-World Assessment of Motor Status After Stroke Using a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface
item.description: A retrospective observational study (n=452) of stroke survivors using home-based BCI therapy found mean UEFM improved by 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001) at week 12, reaching MCID (5.6 points) by week 16, and continued to improve to 8.1 points by week 52.
item.author: medRxiv

item.title: Effectiveness of a Structured Post-Platelet Rich Plasma Rehabilitation Approach on Pain and Function in Subacromial Pain Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description: A randomized controlled trial of 54 SAPS patients found that adding a structured post-PRP rehabilitation approach to conventional physiotherapy significantly improved pain (VAS: 2.92 ± 1.14 vs 7.96 ± 0.75; SF-MPQ: 10.07 ± 3.33 vs 19.37 ± 2.35, p < 0.001) and shoulder function compared to conventional physiotherapy alone over 21 days.
item.author: PubMed
